A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAPA and AI-oversight study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D support comparison, including matching relocated material and identifying actual additions and deletions.

before.justification: v1 reports original metric simulations, judge-bias experiments, weak-to-strong training across 15 tasks and 12 model pairs, and analyses of 130 language models.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds an AlpacaEval preference experiment, further judge-bias analyses, and an independent-error simulation.

M1.justification: CAPA's computation, its existing extensions and negative-domain adjustment, and the weak-to-strong training procedure remain unchanged. The added discussion of regression and alternative priors presents conceptual possibilities without specifying an implemented method change.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds AlpacaEval chat-response preference evaluation using 23 instruction-tuned models, extending coverage beyond correctness judging on filtered MMLU-Pro. The existing MMLU-Pro, BBH, and weak-to-strong task coverage is retained. The simulations also gain an independent-error scenario.

E2.justification: Jensen–Shannon distance is added to the existing agreement/disagreement simulations in Appendix A.7, as verified in v1 Figures 6–8 and v2 Figures 7–9; its earlier use elsewhere is retained. The new independence simulation also evaluates Cohen's kappa and percentage agreement. Existing judge and model rosters remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new chat experiment introduces pairwise preference judging, shuffled preferences, and Elo aggregation over 253 model pairings and 203,665 prompt–pair combinations. Additional analyses restrict comparisons to different model families and control for standardized model size with six outliers excluded. Appendix A.7 adds a 10,000-example simulation varying accuracy over 100 steps; existing training settings remain stable.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial checks of metric validity and judge-bias confounding: independent-error simulation, exclusion of same-family pairs in Figure 3, model-size controls in Appendix B.1, and category-specific analysis addressing aggregation effects in B.5. The earlier weak-to-strong and capability-trend supplementary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a statistical specification controlling for model size and a studentized-residual threshold for excluding six outliers. Existing partial-correlation confidence intervals, significance conventions, and regression diagnostics remain unchanged. No additional repeated-run or seed reporting is documented.

E6.justification: New results include AlpacaEval Elo–CAPA correlations of 0.75–0.87 in Figure 13, size-adjusted regression coefficients in Table 6, category-specific judge correlations, and near-zero CAPA for independent errors in Figure 2. Figure 3 reports a restricted cross-family comparison. The original Table 2 coefficients and Table 3 training gains and ceiling estimates are retained.

T1.justification: The CAPA definitions, derivations, theoretical bounds and proofs, probabilistic agreement variants, and Equation 18 adjustment are unchanged. Added discussion of regression and the uniform prior does not introduce a new formal definition, assumption, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about CAPA, judge affinity bias, complementary knowledge transfer, and increasing error correlation with capability. The new experiments support these claims without redefining the central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendices A.3–A.4 add discussion of possible regression applications and alternatives to the uniform error prior. Appendix B.4 interprets the chat results as initial evidence of cross-task predictive relevance while acknowledging that similarity is measured on MMLU-Pro. Existing causality and free-text limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new simulation and AlpacaEval implementation procedures, but removes v1 Tables 8–16 containing effective sample counts for individual judge–model pairs. Appendix B.9 retains unresolved references to those tables. Existing prompts, training hyperparameters, and code/data links are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds AlpacaFarm, algorithmic-monoculture, and weak-to-strong overfitting references, including Dubois et al. (2023), Kleinberg and Raghavan (2021), and Shi et al. (2025). It modestly expands positioning around homogenization and elicitation ceilings. Most other reference edits update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and section structure remain recognizable. Local revisions expand the metric rationale, clarify weak/strong terminology and ceiling discussion, insert three appendix subsections, and add an impact statement. These are limited revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the independence, AlpacaEval, and category-specific plots and a size-control table; redraws the simulation plots with revised legends and displayed curves; and changes the main judge plot to cross-family pairs. Nine sample-count tables are removed, and numerous retained displays are relocated. This substantially changes the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The new simulation and family-, size-, and category-based checks strengthen support for CAPA and judge affinity bias, while AlpacaEval broadens empirical relevance. These provide a useful incremental improvement to the retained core study. Benefits are moderated by the chat experiment's cross-domain, correlational interpretation and the loss of per-pair sample counts, with broken references remaining in Appendix B.9.
